analysis.one_liner: Let pharmacies buy prescription drugs at discounted federal prices and pass the savings to Medicare beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: The Prescription Drug Fairness Act never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it was introduced less than three months before the 105th Congress ended and died with 64 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Seniors without drug coverage pay the highest prices in the market — often more than twice what big HMOs and hospital chains pay for the same pills. This bill would let any qualified pharmacy sign an agreement with the Secretary of Health and Human Services to buy covered drugs at the discounted prices the federal government already pays on the Federal Supply Schedule, plus a small amount for administrative costs, and sell them to Medicare beneficiaries at that reduced price. Hospices could use the same channel to get cheaper drugs for terminally ill patients. The bill contained no taxpayer spending; the discount came from closing the gap between what drug makers charge seniors and what they charge their biggest customers.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially the roughly senior citizens without any prescription drug coverage, who pay full retail prices that the bill's findings say run more than double the prices drug makers charge their most-favored customers [S3]. Participating pharmacies would gain a new role as the channel for discounted drugs, and hospices could pass lower drug costs to terminal patients [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries paying full drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Any qualified pharmacy could enter an agreement with the Secretary of Health and Human Services to buy covered outpatient drugs at the Federal Supply Schedule price the federal government already pays, and sell them to Medicare beneficiaries at that reduced price [S2].

The bill's findings state that discriminatory pricing means seniors pay over twice what drug manufacturers charge favored customers like HMOs and hospital chains, and that lowering prices for uncovered beneficiaries would improve their health while lowering Medicare costs to taxpayers [S3].
Hospice programs could contract with participating pharmacies to get reduced-price drugs for terminally ill Medicare beneficiaries [S2].
The bill required the Secretary to report annually on whether the Act was protecting beneficiaries from discriminatory pricing, with recommendations for further reductions [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose revenue and margins on sales to seniors would shrink as the gap between senior prices and federal-negotiated prices narrowed. Taxpayers would bear only the Secretary's administrative costs, since the bill authorizes no new benefit payments [S3]. An honest supporter would also acknowledge that manufacturers would likely fight the pricing mechanism, and that pharmacies receive no dispensing fee under the bill, which could limit participation.

drawbacks.text: The bill works by extending federal-negotiated Federal Supply Schedule prices to retail sales, a form of price regulation manufacturers argue could reduce revenue that funds drug research and development [S3].

Pharmacies may purchase only as much of a drug as they sell to Medicare beneficiaries, and the bill provides no dispensing fee for pharmacies, so the participating-pharmacy channel could prove thin if the administrative add-on does not cover pharmacies' costs [S2].
A senior without coverage would still pay out of pocket — the bill lowers the price but creates no insurance benefit, leaving costs to fall fully on the beneficiary [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and direct: seniors paying more than twice the best available price for the same drugs would see substantial savings at no cost to taxpayers beyond administration. The main costs fall on drug manufacturers' senior-market revenue, and the design is lean to a fault — no dispensing fee for pharmacies and no insurance component means the savings reach beneficiaries only if enough pharmacies sign on. On balance it is a simple, low-cost price fix whose main weakness is that it relies on voluntary pharmacy participation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, then to a Commerce subcommittee, and sat there until the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 — no markup, no vote, in either chamber.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Turner introduced the Prescription Drug Fairness Act on September 26, 1998, with 60 original cosponsors listed in the bill text [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and additionally to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
On September 30, 1998, it was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill gathered 64 cosponsors — 63 Democrats and 1 Independent — all from the minority party in the House [S4].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, without the bill receiving a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: the pricing gap the bill targeted — seniors paying over twice what favored customers pay — remained untouched, and no competing legislation from this bill advanced.

for.name: Rep. Jim Turner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the House floor three days after introduction [S5].

for.name: 63 of 207 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to 64 members [S4].

against.name: Thomas Bliley
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral and its Health and Environment Subcommittee took up the bill, but no markup or vote was ever scheduled [S5].

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received a parallel referral and never acted on the bill before Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The bill targeted their pricing practices directly; the industry opposed legislation extending government-negotiated prices to the retail market during this era.

sides.party_line_note: All 64 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-held House never brought the bill to a vote [S4].

industries.note: The bill's stated purpose is to end what it calls discriminatory pricing, under which manufacturers charge seniors more than twice the prices given to HMOs and hospital chains [S3]. Passing it would cut manufacturer revenue on the fast-growing senior market.

Pharmacies would become the delivery channel for discounted drugs, gaining a new purchasing arrangement at federal prices [S2]. But the bill provides no dispensing fee and caps their purchases at what they sell to Medicare beneficiaries, so the benefit to pharmacies is uncertain.
Hospices could procure reduced-price drugs for terminally ill patients through the same program, lowering their costs of care [S2].
